value: actively moving perch spent a significantly higher proportion of time in the chemical stimulus zone when 0.2 ng/ml water-borne cortisol was added than with natural stickleback chemical cues or the water control
units: categorical (proportion of time in stimulus zone; mixed model)
method: behavioural choice test: stimulus water dripped on one side of the perch tank (cortisol, natural chemical cues of sticklebacks, or fresh-water control) with fresh water on the other side, in front of stimulus tanks holding sticklebacks that gave visual cues; time in the chemical stimulus zone scored
conditions: 18 perch collected in October 2010 and 2011 from Howend Trout Fishery (west central Scotland, wild-caught per the Methods), each tested in all three chemosensory tests (54 tests); analysis restricted to actively moving perch (control 16, natural cues 15, cortisol 11); cortisol 0.2 ng/ml free cortisol (Sigma), described as a concentration a predator might encounter in nature; Table 1 gives beta = 0.33, s.e. = 0.09, t = 3.61, P = 0.001; robustness check on the nine perch active in all three treatments (27 trials), duration GLMM t = 3.62, P = 0.002; sticklebacks (150, five per stimulus tank) were wild-caught from Balmaha Pond

source.authors: Henderson LJ, Ryan MR, Rowland HM
source.title: Perch, Perca fluviatilis show a directional preference for, but do not increase attacks toward, prey in response to water-borne cortisol

where: Results, time spent in the chemical stimulus zone (Table 1; Fig. 2A)
quote: When we focus on actively moving individuals, perch spent a significantly higher proportion of their time in the chemical stimulus zone when cortisol was added compared to natural chemical cues of sticklebacks and the water control [...].
note: Classification: behavioural choice of a wild-caught perch to a water-borne chemical cue at a stated concentration; no receptor or sense organ is identified. Cut marked [...]: the trailing '(Table 1 & Fig. 2A)' is dropped; no qualifier is dropped. Nulls and contrary results from the same paper, read as quoted fragments: natural stickleback chemical cues did not differ from the water control; total lunges did not differ between chemosensory tests (GLMM z = -0.35, P = 0.73); movement between zones did not differ (LMM t = 0.38, P = 0.70); the abstract says perch 'did not show a significant increase in total predatory behavior in response to cortisol'; immobility was only marginally more likely with cortisol (P = 0.06). The result holds for actively moving perch only (inactive perch excluded). Perch were collected from a privately owned trout fishery, so the population is fishery-resident, not laboratory-bred. value: scampi in turbulent flow reached the mussel (Perna canaliculus) bait 44% faster and with lower mean heading angles than in laminar flow
units: categorical (time to reach bait; heading angle)
method: flume odour-plume tracking: each scampi released downstream of a 5 g bait in a laminar or turbulent flow regime; 30 min per trial; bait type mussel gonad or jack mackerel tissue
conditions: 100 scampi obtained from 300 m on the Chatham Rise, 250 km off eastern New Zealand, in July 2015 by short-duration bottom trawl and held in individual enclosures in tanks under red light; flume 1.5 x 0.5 x 0.3 m with 10 um and carbon filtered seawater at 10.5 C; 5 g of defrosted bait in a PVC mesh bag at antennule height (a bait mass, not an odour concentration); 60 experiments, 15 per bait-by-flow combination; 28 females and 32 males; flow regime affected heading angle (t 1,38 = 2.78, P = 0.008, both baits) and tortuosity (t 1,38 = 3.04, P = 0.004); numbers reaching the bait 12 (turbulent mussel) and 9 (laminar mussel) as read from the page reader

source.title: Orientation and food search behaviour of a deep sea lobster in turbulent versus laminar odour plumes

quote: Scampi in the turbulent flow reached the mussel bait 44% faster and with lower mean heading angles than in laminar flow.
note: Classification: behavioural response of a wild-caught animal to a bait odour plume; no chemoreceptor is identified and flow regime, not odour concentration, was the manipulated variable. Nulls and contrary results from the same paper, read as quoted fragments: for the mackerel bait the abstract says 'there was no difference between the flow regimes' and the mackerel heading-angle reduction was not significant (t 1,19 = 1.83, P > 0.05); flow regime did not alter success rates for reaching the baits overall (G 1 = 5.03, P > 0.05) or per bait; mean walking speed did not differ between flow regimes; sex and size had no significant effect. value: C. e. ensicauda females were attracted by 10 pmol sodefrin, whereas C. e. popei females were not
method: behavioural attraction test: a plastic container (diameter 37 cm) with 3000 mL tap water, a female newt kept in a steel-mesh cylinder (15 cm diameter) at the centre; synthetic sodefrin applied; attraction scored; Friedman two-way ANOVA then Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test
conditions: sodefrin dose 10 pmol (the minimum effective amount for conspecific females, per the Methods); eight females per subspecies, each test on different specimens (n = 8); females were obtained in February and kept for one month or more in a laboratory vivarium (the page does not say whether they were wild-caught; males of both subspecies were collected in the field from Amami and Okinawa islands); Figure 3 legend: ** p < 0.01; the result is for the subspecies C. e. ensicauda (Amami) and C. e. popei (Okinawa) of one species

value: individuals spent more time with scents of their own (homotypic) population than with scents of another population, independent of sex and population of origin
units: categorical (percentage of observations at each pot)
method: behavioural scent-preference test (Experiment III): two inverted clay pots carrying scents of a homotypic and a heterotypic population placed symmetrically in a round arena; the lizard's side recorded every 30 min over 4.5 h and the percentage of time on each side calculated
conditions: adults collected from the south bank of the Maipo River, central Chile (January 2001, December 2003, February 2004) and housed in the laboratory; 29 trials for L. tenuis in Experiment III (58 trials across both species, as read from the page reader); the Results text prints no statistic for this sentence (Table 3 not read); scent donors not described beyond population of origin; the stimulus is a substrate-borne scent, not a defined compound

source.title: Population Scent Discrimination in Two Liolaemus Lizard Species: Exploring Ethological Isolation

where: Results, 3.3 Experiment III, scent preference for homo- vs. heterotypic mates (Table 3; Figure 5)
quote: Individuals of L. tenuis, independent of their sex and population of origin, spent more time with homotypic scents (Table 3; Figure 5).
note: Classification: behavioural choice between substrate-borne scents; the chemical nature of the cue is assumed by the author, no compound is identified. Contrary and null results from the same paper, read as quoted fragments: in Experiment I L. tenuis explored heterotypic scents more than homotypic scents (more tongue flicks) and did not distinguish the two heterotypic populations, while latency to the first tongue flick and motion time were not affected by scent origin; the Discussion reads the higher tongue-flick rate toward heterotypic scents as perception of a different scent. In Experiment II L. tenuis spent more time, tongue-flicked more and moved more near homotypic scents (summary from the page reader). The sibling species L. lemniscatus showed weak or nonexistent discrimination and is not filed.
